title: How Rockets Work
tagline: From Newton's third law to a full-flow engine and a booster that lands. Learn it by taking the hardware apart.
audience: Curious adults with no engineering background who want to understand how modern rockets such as SpaceX's Starship actually work
prerequisites: School-level ideas of force, mass and pressure; no maths beyond multiplying and dividing
outcomes: Explain why a rocket accelerates, in space as well as in air
Use the rocket equation to say why most of a rocket is propellant
Trace oxygen and methane through a full-flow staged-combustion engine, part by part
Explain why rockets drop stages, and how a booster flies back and lands
Read a rocket's spec sheet and check its numbers with back-of-envelope arithmetic

glossary.thrust: the force the engine pushes the rocket with, given here in tonnes-force (tf): 1 tf holds up 1 tonne against Earth's gravity
glossary.chamber pressure: the pressure of the burning gas inside the main combustion chamber, in bar (1 bar is about atmospheric pressure at sea level)
glossary.preburner: a small combustion chamber that burns a little propellant to make hot gas for a turbine
glossary.turbopump: a turbine and a pump on one shaft: hot gas spins the turbine, the pump forces propellant into the engine
glossary.mixture ratio: kilograms of oxygen burned per kilogram of fuel

chapters.title: Why rockets fly
chapters.summary: A rocket throws mass backwards fast and is pushed forwards in return. It needs nothing to push against, so it works best in a vacuum.
outcomes: Explain thrust as momentum thrown backwards
Say why a rocket needs no air to push against

figures.concept: thrust comes from mass thrown backwards
figures.object: a small engine on a thrust stand with a load cell and a propellant tank on a scale

chapters.title: The rocket equation
chapters.summary: Every bit of speed costs propellant, and the propellant has to lift itself. That is why more than nine tenths of a rocket on the pad is propellant.
outcomes: Use Δv = vₑ ln(m₀/m₁) with real numbers

figures.concept: each step of speed costs a fixed fraction of the remaining mass
figures.object: a stack of propellant tanks on a scale beside a small payload, draining one by one

chapters.title: Inside the engine
chapters.summary: A rocket engine is a pump problem. SpaceX's Raptor burns a little of each propellant just to drive its pumps, and nothing is thrown away.
outcomes: Trace oxygen and methane through a full-flow staged-combustion engine
Explain why the pumps, not the fire, are the hard part
Check an engine's spec sheet with thrust = flow × exhaust speed

figures.concept: both propellants drive their own pump on the way to the chamber
figures.object: Raptor 2 on a vertical test stand, taken apart part by part and fired

chapters.title: Staging and reuse
chapters.summary: Dropping empty tanks is the cheapest way to go faster. Bringing the booster back is how you stop paying for it every flight.
outcomes: Explain why two stages beat one
Describe how a booster flies back and is caught or lands

figures.concept: an empty stage is dead weight
figures.object: a two-stage stack on a launch mount that separates in flight

chapters.title: Steering
chapters.summary: Rockets steer by pointing their engines. Grid fins take over when the booster falls back through the air.
outcomes: Explain thrust vectoring with a gimballed engine
Say when grid fins help and when they can't

figures.concept: tilting the engine turns the rocket
figures.object: an engine on a gimbal with two actuators under a pivoting stage

chapters.title: Getting to orbit
chapters.summary: Orbit is falling and missing the ground. It takes about 7.8 km/s sideways at low altitude, which is why going up is the easy part.
outcomes: Estimate the speed needed for low Earth orbit
